title: Key locations
description: The charged non-settlement places a finished world implies: caves, mines, barrows, mausoleums, shrines, watchtowers, ley nexuses, lairs, drowned ruins and wonders. Produced by the standalone key_locations package, which reads the finished world JSON and mutates nothing, so the world's own recipe, replay identity and native parity are untouched. FANTASY_WORLD_KEY_LOCATIONS=0 leaves the key absent.

version.description: 2: a percentile requirement whose resolved cut admits every cell in the archetype's own domain is refused, so no site is emitted through a gate that enforced nothing. Sites disappear across this boundary that a version-1 consumer saw; the counts are not comparable.

error.description: Present only when status is failed; the block is reported, never raised.

catalogue_count.description: Archetypes in the catalogue, not locations placed.

dungeons.description: Tier-2 complexes with a hostile occupant. There is no dungeon archetype; this is what the word means here.

families.description: Display metadata per family: name, glyph, colour, spacing.

id.description: Derived from where the place is, never from where it landed in a list. Node sites: keyloc-<archetype>-<node>. Chain members: keyloc-<archetype>-<chain key>-<metres along it>. Cluster members: keyloc-<archetype>-<anchor node>-<offset>-<index>. None of them renumber when the block is re-derived on advance_age_request, so a foreign key survives. Stable is not immortal: if an age transition drowns a location or destroys the culture that justified it, the location legitimately ceases to exist and the id resolves to nothing. Treat a dangling key as "the place is gone", not as renumbering.

kind.description: Archetype id, e.g. silver_mine, karst_cave, mausoleum.

name.description: Unique within a world. Descriptor templates filled from world facts, in the same idiom hero_generator uses for sites.

tier.description: PHYSICAL SCALE AND BUILD-OUT ONLY - never danger. 0 a marker with no interior ever; 1 a one-scene site; 2 a multi-room complex that always has an interior; 3 a unique world-scale wonder. A tier-3 wonder may be harmless and a tier-1 barrow lethal: read threat for danger. Unrelated to the three other 'tier' fields in this tree - creature tier (int 1-5 danger, terrain_nest_profiles.json), villain tier (float standing that also sets reach in metres, terrain_villains.py) and hero tier (string enum notable/renowned/legendary, hero-generator.schema.json).

threat.description: Danger, on the same 1-5 creature-tier rubric the nest catalogue uses: 1 harmless, 5 a campaign threat. Derived from occupant class, state, tier, local weave instability and the tier of any nest nearby. Travel distance is deliberately not included - that is a function of where the party is.

state.description: Derived, not authored: a nearby ruin ages a site, remoteness empties it, an unstable weave corrupts it, passing ages wear it down. 'natural' is for geology, which has no builders to leave. A 'forgotten fortress' is state ruined with occupant none.

occupant.description: Who is there now, derived from state, remoteness and what lives nearby.

node.description: Sphere-grid node id, as every other point record in the world uses.

suitability_factors.description: Per-term breakdown of the score, for explainability.

ruin_id.description: The fallen city this location belongs to, when one is near enough to explain it.

school.description: Dominant magic school of the ground.

succession.description: Set when something moved in after the builders left, which is where dungeons come from. Recorded rather than silently overwriting the occupant, so a consumer can say 'a goblin warren that used to be a silver mine'.

chain_index.description: Position along the chain, counted from its start. Ordered, not arbitrary.

reason.description: One sentence saying why this place is here.

interior.description: Present on every tier-2 site and on nothing else. A GRAPH, NOT GEOMETRY: chambers carry depth, role, rough size and connections, with no metre positions, no contents and no encounters. A real interior layout is a later phase.

placement.description: How this location was positioned. "node" sites sit on a sphere-grid node and no two of them ever share one. "path" members belong to a chain and stand at interpolated points along a road, a frontier or an approach - a waystone every 2 km cannot be node-snapped on a 12 km raster - and "cluster" members stand at a real offset from an anchor. Both of the latter may share a node with each other; their node is for reading layers, not identity.

environment.description: The ground this location stands on, for whoever has to dress it. All of it is in the layers already; it is recorded here so an art pipeline never has to re-sample a raster it otherwise never touches. The same karst cave is a different art set in tundra and in rainforest.

natural_biome.description: Natural catalogue ID from terrain.natural_biomes, per terrain.biome_contract: an id, never an array offset. The id space is sparse - 0-8, 13, 15, 16, 17 - so a 0-12 bound rejected marsh, boreal forest, cold tundra and persistent land ice. Decides the ground set.

biome_variant.description: Index into terrain.magical_biomes where the ground is magically mutated, null where it is not. Overrides the natural biome for dressing.

chains.description: Ordered runs of markers along something the world already has. A lone waystone is noise; eleven counting down to a shrine is a story.

kind.description: The chain spec that produced it.

name.description: A type label ("Waystone line"), not a proper noun.

interval_m.description: Absolute metres, deliberately unscaled: how far apart people set waystones is a fact about people, not about world size.

anchor.description: The site the chain leads to, for an approach.

members.description: Site ids in walk order, start to end.

clusters.description: Sites that hang off an anchor already placed: a siege camp outside a ruined fort, cottages beside a mine, barrows ringing a necropolis.

anchor.description: Site id of what explains this cluster.

diagnostics.description: One row per *pass*, not one per archetype - an archetype declaring also_scatters produces two - including the passes that placed nothing and why. A world with no volcanism reports the gap rather than approximating around it. Four gap reasons point at four different people: the world never generated the layer; this world has no cells of that domain; the layer is identically constant across the domain, which is a catalogue fault no seed or raster can rescue; and the percentile resolved to a cut admitting the whole domain, which is a distribution too piled up at one end for a nearest-rank cut to divide.
